summary.title: Learnings from 5 years of tech startup code audits
summary.one_liner: Lessons from roughly two dozen security code audits of startups, covering which engineering choices, vulnerability types, and review practices mattered most in practice.
takeaways: Simple architectures tended to outperform clever or microservice-heavy designs for the startups audited.
Discoverability matters more than exploit cleverness: the worst bugs were easy to find and exploit.
Never deserialize untrusted objects; prefer JSON and manually construct objects from fields.
Secure-by-default frameworks (e.g., React escaping, serverless) reduced attack surface compared with older stacks like PHP.
Custom fuzzing of product APIs and auth was surprisingly efficient; many JWT and webhook implementations were flawed, and many MD5 findings were false positives.
summary.summary: The author, who led a security practice at PKC, shares lessons from 20-30 code audits, mostly of startups around Series A or B. The post is a list of about 15 observations, ordered from general engineering lessons to security-specific ones. Topics include team size, simplicity versus cleverness, where high-impact findings appear, and how framework defaults and monorepos affect security. It also covers dependency risk, deserialization, business logic flaws, custom fuzzing, JWT and webhook mistakes, and MD5 false positives. The examples are anecdotal and the author says the evidence is not statistically rigorous.
